demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
Patient: Mrs. L., a 60-year-old, married woman of South Eastern Asian descent.
Occupation: Call center agent for a major telecommunications company.
Chief Complaint: "I can't stop thinking about my sister, and I can't sleep."

Mrs. L. sits forward in the chair, her hands clasped tightly in her lap. She speaks in a low, measured tone, but her eyes are bright with unshed tears. She begins her story not with the trauma, but with the day before it.

"My younger sister, Srey, she lived in Phnom Penh. We spoke every Sunday. It was our ritual. She would call me, and I would be here, in my little home office, just like I am for work. We would talk for an hour. About her garden, about my son, about the food she was cooking."

The Sunday that changed everything was three months ago. The call came, but it was not Srey. It was her neighbor, speaking in a frantic, broken voice. Srey had collapsed at the market. A stroke. By the time Mrs. L. could arrange a flight, Srey was gone.

"I didn't get to say goodbye," she whispers. "I was on the phone with a customer, helping them with their internet bill, when it happened. I was... solving a problem. While my sister was dying. I didn't know. I was just... working."

The memory of that phone call is now a permanent, jagged scar. She cannot hear the specific hold music of her company without a jolt of adrenaline. The cheerful, automated voice that says "Your call is important to us" now feels like a mockery.

At work, Mrs. L. is a ghost of her former self. She was once the top performer on her team, known for her patience and her ability to de-escalate angry customers. Now, she struggles. Her voice, once warm, is flat. She has to mute her headset multiple times a day to take a slow, deep breath. A customer's complaint about a late bill can trigger a wave of nausea, because the sound of an angry voice-any angry voice-is the sound of the neighbor's frantic tone on the phone that day.

Her home life is similarly fractured. Her husband, a kind man, tries to help, but she pushes him away. Their bed is a battlefield. She cannot sleep. Every time she closes her eyes, she sees Srey's face, but not as she was. She sees her as she imagines her: alone, on the ground, in a crowded market. She has vivid, intrusive images of the scene she never witnessed. She has started sleeping on the couch in the living room, because the bedroom is too quiet, and the quiet lets the images in.

The most difficult symptom for her is the avoidance. She has not answered her phone in months. She lets all calls go to voicemail. The sound of a ringing phone-her cell phone, the landline, even a phone in a movie-makes her heart pound so hard she feels she might faint. She has disconnected her home office line, forcing her to use a different, less familiar headset for work. Her Sunday ritual is gone. She has not spoken to Srey's other friends. She cannot bring herself to look at any photos.

She is constantly on guard. A sudden loud noise-a car backfiring, a door slamming-makes her flinch. She feels a pervasive sense of dread, as if another terrible piece of news is waiting for her just around the corner. She describes it as "a crack in the world that I keep falling into." The world, once predictable and orderly, now feels brittle and dangerous.

She came to therapy because her supervisor at work issued a formal warning about her declining performance. She is terrified of losing her job, the one thing that gives her structure. But more than that, she is terrified of the silence. The silence on the other end of the phone line, where her sister's voice used to be.
